doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: World music sparked by Coltrane
summary: A Coltrane trill on The Last Train led Levy to Middle Eastern, African, Indonesian and Indian music in the 1970s.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: It’s unbelievable. And there’s this blues called “By the Numbers.” Red Garland plays like the most amazing blues jazz piano solos. Like perfect and beautiful. And Coltrane comes in on his solo and plays this one little figure [scats] it’s like a little trill [scats]. It’s obviously not jazz. It’s obviously from another culture. He was invoking another world and that piqued my curiosity. And that one little figure he played led me to explore Middle Eastern music and Eastern European music and then eventually African music and Indonesian and Balinese Gamelan and Indian music and like I didn’t own a TV for about six years. I got sort of disgusted with American pop culture in the ‘70s and polyester clothes and all that stuff. And I just got into the roots of music. You know? Like what is underlying things. You know I just took a deep dive into it and bought as many albums as I could and took out records from the Evanston Library and recorded them onto a reel to reel tape recorder and just listened over and over again, and went to as many concerts of world music, ethnic music – whatever you want to call it – as I could. Yeah. So yeah.
That leads me to – this could be a Name that Tune or blindfold test. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
